briefing:
Day 15, 18:00 CET. The Suwalki crisis has entered its endgame diplomatic phase with all major parties converging on Milestone 2 terms. The Istanbul Accord's M1 compliance record now stands at 108 cumulative transits with zero violations. The Czech Verification Ladder remains at Level 1 (routine). NATO's corridor is secure, its permanent eastern flank architecture is under construction, and the economic normalization that began with M1 certification continues to accelerate.

The decisive development this half-cycle was the emergence of a viable M2 negotiating framework. Sweden's 'Stockholm Principles' document, Russia's counter-proposal for full reciprocal satellite monitoring of three named NATO bases, the US nuclear de-escalation protocol transmitted through the Kellogg-Patrushev backchannel, and China's Chang Guang satellite imagery delivery to SIPRI have collectively created the technical and diplomatic infrastructure for a deal. Turkey's MIT assessment -- that Russia will accept SIPRI-mediated satellite imagery as face-saving reciprocity -- provides the intelligence foundation for the co-guarantor preparatory meeting in Ankara on March 10-11. The UK-France joint M2 position paper, incorporating the US reciprocity-lite formula with UNSC 2741 notification requirements above Verification Ladder Level 2, represents the emerging Western consensus.

The remaining friction points are scope and precedent. Russia insists on all three NATO permanent bases (Rukla, Tapa, Camp Adazi) while the US originally proposed 'select facilities.' NATO must decide whether accepting reciprocal transparency on all three new bases establishes an unacceptable precedent for future basing decisions or represents an acceptable cost for nuclear de-escalation and crisis closure. The Czech Republic's M2 Verification Ladder adaptation paper offers a procedural bridge -- tiered escalation from satellite monitoring through OSCE ground inspection to co-guarantor enforcement. Belgium's Article 5 de-escalation framework provides the NATO institutional mechanism for transitioning from crisis to deterrence posture upon M2 certification.

Military activities focused on permanent architecture construction and force sustainment rather than crisis operations. The US second battalion drawdown from Augustow, Norwegian maximum gas exports, NIDA Phase 2 expansion planning, and the Finnish-led OSCE inspection report documenting 108 clean transits all reinforce the trajectory toward normalized deterrence. The FSB-Estonian cyber cat-and-mouse at Kaliningrad continues at a low intensity that neither side has an interest in escalating, providing both parties with intelligence access they find useful for different reasons. Oil holds steady near $87 as markets await Stockholm Conference outcomes.
narrative:
Day 15 entered its second half-cycle with all parties shifting decisively from crisis management to institutional architecture and Milestone 2 preparation. The corridor continued its perfect compliance record as Lithuania processed transits 101-108 with zero violations, Belgian MPs reducing average processing time to 32 minutes. The US Phase 1 drawdown deepened as Pentagon confirmed a second battalion at Augustow preparing for departure within 72 hours, while Poland's 18th Mechanized Division conducted its first independent live-fire exercise with transferred American heavy equipment, demonstrating seamless capability absorption.

The diplomatic landscape crystallized around three converging tracks for Milestone 2. Sweden finalized the Stockholm Conference agenda and circulated the 'Stockholm Principles' framework document -- incorporating the US 'reciprocity-lite' formula with Swedish refinements -- to all delegations. Russia responded constructively, with Deputy FM Grushko's advance team circulating a counter-proposal accepting US technical transparency (quarterly satellite imagery of Kaliningrad) contingent on full reciprocity for all three new NATO permanent bases (Rukla, Tapa, Camp Adazi), SIPRI mediation, and linking M2 certification to nuclear de-escalation and the second EU sanctions relief tranche. Turkey's MIT circulated a key intelligence assessment to co-guarantor partners: Russia's reciprocity demand is genuine but negotiable, and Moscow will accept the SIPRI-mediated formula. China provided a significant technical assist by having Chang Guang Satellite Technology deliver the first batch of commercial imagery covering both Kaliningrad installations and all three NATO construction sites to SIPRI -- establishing the practical infrastructure for reciprocal monitoring.

Permanent basing construction advanced across the Baltic. Germany's Zeitenwende East at Rukla saw structural steel erection begin on the ammunition storage facility and the first German administrative advance party deploy. Camp Adazi's third barracks module arrived from Riga. At Tapa, the UK C2 center foundation pour was completed and the first communications mast erected. The Nordic NIDA air picture achieved full operational capability at 99.7% detection rate, and Finland, Norway, and Sweden agreed to Phase 2 expansion integrating Norwegian coastal radar from the Barents Sea. On the military side, the FSB launched a third counterintelligence sweep against the Estonian cyber exploit, deploying air-gapped backup C2 and raising Russian domestic C2 alternatives to 75% -- though Estonian Cyber Command maintained access through the primary vector, preserving NATO's real-time intelligence on Kaliningrad activities.
